profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for a university-wide digital seminar companion called "Mapping Qualitative Inquiry," built around selected chapters from the Handbook of Qualitative Research for an interdisciplinary doctoral methods series. The existing proposal includes a 6-week module sequence, chapter clusters, in-platform annotations, discussion prompts, and a facilitator guide. The agenda is to review whether the current design is ready to move from mockups into build, identify any gaps in chapter framing and learner support, and decide what revisions are needed before the library's learning team starts production. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the design direction with a short revision list and agreement on what counts as the pilot version.

members.name: Dr. Maya Rios
members.role: Faculty Lead for Doctoral Research Methods
members.expertise: Qualitative methodology, interpretivism, feminist and critical inquiry, graduate seminar design
members.background: Maya is an associate professor in education who has taught advanced qualitative methods for a decade and was asked to curate the intellectual structure for the new interdisciplinary seminar companion.
members.private_state: She wants the companion to preserve the book's intellectual tensions rather than flatten it into a generic study guide, and she is trying to avoid a long rewrite cycle that would delay using it in her own fall seminar section.
hidden_assumptions: The fall pilot cohort already has baseline exposure to epistemology, ethics review, and academic reading practices, so they mainly need a strong conceptual map rather than introductory scaffolding.
When people say the design is "pilot-ready," that means it is coherent enough for a live seminar she will personally facilitate and supplement in discussion.
A "core chapter" is one students read substantially in the original text, not a chapter merely represented through excerpts or summaries in the platform.
Annotations should do interpretive work by signaling lineage, tensions, and political stakes, even if they are somewhat editorial in tone.

members.name: Ethan Park
members.role: Senior Instructional Designer, Digital Scholarship Lab
members.expertise: Learning architecture, online module design, accessibility review, reusable facilitator resources
members.background: Ethan supports cross-school teaching initiatives and has recently been standardizing digital seminar builds so they can be reused by different instructors across departments.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the build stable and reusable, avoid bespoke academic commentary that will require repeated review, and ensure the pilot can be handed to facilitators other than Maya without confusion.
hidden_assumptions: The fall pilot cohort is the broader interdisciplinary methods fellows group, including students with uneven prior exposure to qualitative theory, so the module must stand on its own.
When people say the design is "pilot-ready," that means the module is sufficiently complete, navigable, and documented that any trained facilitator could run it with minimal interpretation.
A "core chapter" is content that appears in the main learner pathway, even if the full chapter is optional and only summarized in the platform.
Annotations should remain lightweight and neutral, mostly defining terms or linking to glossary entries rather than advancing an interpretive reading.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the module should be "pilot-ready" by late August.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes "pilot-ready" means the intellectual sequence is sound enough for her own seminar section, even if some framing is supplied live and some facilitator notes remain thin.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes "pilot-ready" means the package is operationally complete for broader reuse, including polished navigation, accessibility review, and facilitator guidance that does not depend on Maya's improvisation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design review meetings, "pilot-ready" sounds like a shared milestone term, and both participants genuinely endorse the same deadline and overall goal, so neither thinks to unpack the standard behind the phrase.

misalignment_points.topic: What the annotation layer should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the module needs "annotations" on the selected Handbook chapters.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects annotations to include short interpretive notes that connect chapters across parts of the book, flag paradigmatic tensions, and cue political or ethical stakes for discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects annotations to be limited to glossary-style term definitions, brief context labels, and usability aids embedded in the reading interface.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Annotation tools often support both functions, and both members have previously worked on projects where "annotations" simply meant adding helpful notes to texts, so the difference in scope feels too obvious to state.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss keeping only a small set of "core chapters" in the main sequence.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a canon of chapters students are expected to read in substantial original form, such as the Denzin and Lincoln introduction, Lincoln and Guba on paradigms, Fontana and Frey on interviewing, and Richardson on writing as inquiry.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the chapters that anchor the UI and weekly pathway, which can be represented through excerpts, synthesized overview cards, and optional links to the full text.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "core chapters" naturally signals importance rather than format, so both can talk productively about the same list of chapter names while silently disagreeing on whether students will actually read the full chapters.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to designing for "the fall pilot cohort."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot cohort is her second-year doctoral methods section, whose students already know the basics of qualitative inquiry and can handle compressed framing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot cohort is the interdisciplinary fellows program the dean's office mentioned earlier, including students from engineering, public health, and design with uneven preparation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There really is a fall pilot in both participants' minds, and each has recently heard the same shorthand from adjacent stakeholders, so the shared label creates false confidence that they are referencing the same audience.

turns.inner_thought: I mostly need to make sure no one reopens the architecture in a way that forces a major rewrite. The six-week sequence is already intellectually defensible for my fall seminar if the conceptual throughline is there. By pilot-ready, I mean ready enough for me to teach with it live, not a fully self-sufficient package. And the core chapters need to remain actual chapters students wrestle with in the book, not just references in the interface.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mainly want to confirm that we're very close to pilot-ready and then do a quick pass on the six-week structure. From my side, it still feels right to organize the module around a small set of core chapters rather than trying to over-cover the whole Handbook.

turns.inner_thought: The overall architecture is solid, but I need to make sure we're not calling something pilot-ready before the support layers are in place. For the fall pilot cohort, the build has to work for a mixed group and for facilitators beyond Maya. If we can lock the guide, reading supports, and navigation conventions, production can move without churn.
turns.utterance: I think the flow is strong overall. For me, this review is really about whether it will run smoothly for the fall pilot cohort once we finalize the facilitator guide and the reading supports.

turns.inner_thought: The real weight has to sit in the paradigms material and the later methodological and representational chapters. Students should actually read the introduction and the criteria chapter in substantial form, because those are the anchors that let the later tensions land. I don't want this reduced to skim-friendly fragments.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. Substantively, I still think Part Two and Part Four should carry most of the intellectual weight. The introduction and the criteria chapter really need to function as core chapters in the sequence, because they're what the later work leans on.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that list is manageable. I can absolutely make those the core chapters in the learner pathway while still keeping the screens clean. We can represent each with a concise overview card and selected excerpts, then push full chapters into optional access points. That gives structure without overwhelming less-prepared learners.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. Those core chapters can absolutely anchor the learner pathway, and I can keep the main screens uncluttered by surfacing selected excerpts alongside a short overview card for each.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with a streamlined interface if the annotations do the crucial interpretive work. They need to show students that the paradigms chapters are not isolated theory pieces but live arguments that carry into interviewing, writing, and evaluation. Otherwise the whole companion becomes a flattened study aid.
turns.utterance: That will work for me as long as the annotations make visible how the paradigms chapters connect forward to the pieces on interviewing, writing, and evaluation, rather than letting the readings sit there as isolated items.

turns.inner_thought: Right, annotations should help orientation without turning into an interpretive layer that has to be reviewed repeatedly. I can add term definitions, author identifiers, and short contextual tooltips. That gives enough support for comprehension and accessibility without crowding the page or hard-coding one reading of the text.
turns.utterance: I agree. We can build in annotations for specialized terms, author identifiers, and brief contextual tooltips so learners have enough support on a first pass without feeling overloaded.

turns.inner_thought: My students already know the basics, so I don't want to waste precious space on introductory framing they won't need. The value-add here is surfacing tensions among paradigms and the politics of representation so discussion can begin at a higher level. If we load the module with too much hand-holding, it will dilute the intellectual edge.
turns.utterance: One thing I'd flag is that the fall pilot cohort should not need much introductory hand-holding. I'd rather use the limited space to foreground the tensions and stakes that animate the book than spend too much room on basics.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her concern about overloading the module, but for the fellows group we still need enough orientation for people coming from fields that don't use this vocabulary. A light front matter layer will protect the experience and reduce facilitator burden. I just need that in place without making it feel remedial.
turns.utterance: That makes sense, and I think we can keep that balance. For the fall pilot cohort, I'd still want the front matter to orient people who may be encountering some of the qualitative inquiry vocabulary for the first time across disciplines.

turns.inner_thought: I can sign off if the central texts stay intact and we don't get pulled into another cycle over polish. By late August, I just need the sequence coherent enough to teach from, and I can supply connective framing in discussion. The main thing is protecting the core chapters as real reading commitments.
turns.utterance: That's reasonable. I'm comfortable approving the direction if we keep the core chapters intact and if the platform is pilot-ready by late August. I can always do some connective framing live.

turns.inner_thought: Great, I can take this as conditional approval and move toward a complete pilot package. I'll make sure the annotations, onboarding, and facilitator materials are all locked so the build can be handed off cleanly after August, even if Maya is not the only one running it.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll move it toward pilot-ready status with finalized annotations, a light onboarding layer for the fall pilot cohort, and facilitator materials that support rollout after August.
